uncited: It builds on [Simplified Phong Lighting Model](885-simplified-phong-lighting-model.md) by introducing this half-vector approximation for the specular term.
*   Position of the shading point $P$ (in world or texture space).
*   Surface normal $\mathbf{n}$ (normalized gradient vector for volume data).
*   Light position $\mathbf{l}_{pos}$ and light intensity/color $I_L$.
*   Camera/Eye position $\mathbf{e}_{pos}$.
*   Shininess exponent $n$ (controls specular lobe width).
*   Material coefficients: ambient $k_a$, diffuse $k_d$, specular $k_s$.
*   Base color/transfer function output $C_{base}$.
*   Vectors $\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{h}$ are 3D floating-point vectors.
*   Scalars $n, k_a, k_d, k_s, I_L$ are floating-point values.
[Note: Some implementations define $\mathbf{v}$ as pointing towards the eye, others away.
The dot product $\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}$ requires $\mathbf{l}$ to point from surface to light.
The half-vector definition $\mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v})$ assumes both point away from the surface or both towards, depending on convention.
Standard Blinn-Phong uses vectors pointing *away* from the surface for $\mathbf{l}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, or *towards* for both.
The half vector is $\mathbf{H} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{V})$.
This is consistent if $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{V}$ are both defined as directions from the surface.]
Higher values produce sharper highlights.
*   **Time Complexity:** $O(1)$ per shading point.
It involves a few vector normalizations, dot products, and a power function.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(1)$ auxiliary memory.
*   **Strengths:** Computationally inexpensive; provides visually plausible specular highlights; widely supported in hardware (fragment shaders).
*   **When to use:** Real-time volume rendering where performance is critical and approximate specular highlights are desired.
*   **When not to use:** When physically accurate light transport, shadows, or global illumination are required.
